summary: Proposes organizing internet host names into hierarchical name domains, so that every host does not need to be listed in every table. It aims to fit existing mail systems and scale to thousands of hosts.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of one giant address book listing everyone, split it into sections like school, company and club. This memo suggests that for naming computers.

questions: what is the internet mailbox name syntax
subtitle: A 1981 proposal to split the flat list of internet host names into name domains, with mail forwarders that know each domain's hosts.

tldr.problem: Every internet host was expected to keep every other host in its name-address table. With over four hundred names and nicknames in the combined ARPANET-DCNET tables, that was already awkward.
tldr.mechanism: Hosts are grouped into name domains such as ARPA or COMSAT. Each domain has mail forwarder processes that hold its host table, and a mailbox is named user.host@domain.
tldr.outcome: The memo is offered to stimulate discussion and says the scheme is believed compatible with existing mail systems and extensible to thousands of hosts.

today: The unit metadata gives no status for RFC 799 and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text calls itself a proposal meant to stimulate discussion.

sections.title: The Problem of Flat Name Tables
sections.content:
In the long run, it will not be practicable for every internet host to include all internet hosts in its name-address tables. The author notes that some hierarchical partitioning of the name space is easy to devise, but it was wickedly difficult to find one compatible with the mail systems known across the community.

The scheme proposed here came out of several discussions and meetings and is believed both compatible with existing systems and extensible for thousands of hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: One address book listing every computer gets too big to keep, so it needs to be split up.

sections.title: Name Domains and Forwarders
sections.content:
Every internet host is identified by one or more 32-bit internet addresses. The memo lays a set of name domains over the space of addresses. In the natural model a domain matches an institution such as ARPA, UCL or COMSAT. Domains need not be disjoint or complete, and the memo assumes only a single-level structure.

Each domain is served by one or more mail forwarder processes, and the domain's name is the name of any of them. A forwarder keeps duplicate tables naming all hosts in its domain, plus at least one forwarder for every other domain. Every host keeps at least one forwarder for every domain, and a host may belong to several domains. Multi-homed hosts can use any of their addresses for mail.
sections.plainLanguage: Each section of the address book has a helper. The helper knows everyone in the section, and knows who the other sections' helpers are.

sections.title: Mailbox Names and Examples
sections.content:
The general standard internet mailbox name is <user>.<host>@<domain>, a three-level name read from the right. Hosts in one domain may agree on another structure if it does not conflict and the forwarders can make the transformations. For example, Mills@COMSAT-DLM works inside the COMSAT domain, while Mills.COMSAT-DLM@COMSAT works from anywhere.

A typical set of domains might include ARPA, COMSAT, DCA, UCL, MIT, INTELPOST and the public data networks. The ARPA forwarder would build its table from the latest HOSTS.TXT in the NIC data base, and other forwarders would deposit a copy of theirs there.
sections.plainLanguage: An address says who, which computer, and which section, in that order. Inside your own section a shorter form can work.

sections.title: Relays, Routes and Header Editing
sections.content:
Most mail is expected to go directly from sender host to recipient host. Some messages need an intermediate mail relay, for example when the two hosts are not up at the same time, or do not share the same lower-level transport (such as TCP and NCP). Every forwarder is a relay, but not every relay is a forwarder.

The sender picks the relay sequence with the source route in the MRCP command, and advisory messages return along that route in reverse. When a host serves several domains, a name like Mills@HOST can be ambiguous, so the memo says the full name .<host>@<domain> is required for relay hosts and that the sending host must update the sender-route as well. It follows the RFC 780 mail model.

The memo advises avoiding edits to the RFC 733 header. Where unavoidable, as on many ARPANET hosts, editing should happen on first entry to the internet mail system. It closes by saying it is meant to stimulate discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail usually goes straight to the person, but sometimes it has to stop at a post office on the way. The full address stops the post office from guessing wrong.

references.text: The MTP mail model referred to in the text as RFC-780.
